Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure.
  - 7 days of fever with alternating hot/cold sweats, generalized myalgias, nausea with reduced oral intake.
  - Recent travel: Returned from Vietnam 4 weeks ago; toured multiple regions including countryside; trekking and cycling through farmland. Took malaria prophylaxis daily; may have taken an additional medication (names not recalled).
- Symptom timeline and progression.
  - Onset ~7 days ago; persistent symptoms with intermittent temperature fluctuations. Partial, temporary relief with over-the-counter antipyretics.
- ENT symptoms (as applicable): throat swelling/closure sensation, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face), ear/neck symptoms.
  - Denies cough/cold/sore throat.
  - Denies ear pain.
  - Denies neck stiffness.
  - No rash noted.
  - Headache: longstanding, centrally located, related to screen use/weather; no new or severe headache reported.
  - No documentation of throat tightness/closure sensation, voice change/hoarseness, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea, facial/oral/uvular swelling, hearing change, or neck swelling.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments (including any prior hospital care or injection therapy).
  - No prior similar episodes documented. No ED visits/hospitalizations mentioned.
- Allergies and current medications (mark missing dose/route/frequency as not documented).
  - Allergies: Pollen (hay fever). No medication allergies reported.
  - Medications: Seroxat (dose/route/frequency not documented). Over-the-counter ibuprofen and paracetamol at “recommended dose” (specific dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Any relevant social context (e.g., accompaniment/supervision).
  - Works as a nurse; currently struggling at work due to fatigue. Up to date with vaccinations including Hepatitis B. Non-smoker; moderate alcohol intake. Plans to attend central London clinic today.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution (e.g., lips, tongue, uvula, face) if stated.
  - Not stated.
- Airway/breathing descriptors if stated (e.g., stridor, work of breathing).
  - Not stated.
- Mental status and associated features (e.g., dizziness, syncope) if stated.
  - Not stated.
- Vitals and examination findings only if mentioned; otherwise note “Not recorded.”
  - Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient (if stated).
  - Not stated.

Assessment:
- Febrile illness without clear ENT focus; recent travel to Vietnam with rural exposure. Concern raised for malaria or other travel-related infection. No current ENT localizing symptoms or red flags reported.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised.
  - Arrange in-person clinical examination today at a central London clinic; clinician to message admin to book.
  - Patient instructed to call the number placed in the consultation notes after a few minutes to be scheduled.
  - Pre-requested investigations to include thick and thin blood films for malaria and inflammatory markers (exact tests per clinician note).
  - If unable to attend central London, advised to attend a local A&E (emergency department).
  - Advised not to go to work until the cause is identified and managed.
- Specific instructions provided to patient/caregiver.
  - Bring/show the typed consultation notes at reception.
  - Call the provided number to be slotted into clinic.
- Escalation criteria/red flags.
  - Not documented in the transcript.
- Follow-up.
  - Follow-up contingent on findings of in-person examination and blood tests. No ENT/allergy referral discussed.
- COVID-19 vaccine suitability.
  - Not discussed.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements for an acute ENT/allergy presentation:
  - Detailed ENT airway symptoms (throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling, stridor, dyspnea), facial/oral/uvular swelling, nasal/ocular symptoms, hearing changes.
  - Objective exam, vitals, and temperature measurements.
  - Complete drug/food allergy list; medication doses/routes/frequencies.
  - Prior severe reactions, prior ED visits/hospitalizations, availability of rescue medications or devices.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - None clinically significant. (Clinician used “sir” once despite patient identified as female; not medically relevant.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; some pauses and incomplete sentences; adequate for clinical documentation.
